lesson.title: The Local Test, One Point at a Time
lesson.summary: Reduces differentiability at a single point to comparing one-sided derivatives at a seam, worked through a piecewise function that is continuous but has mismatched slopes at x = 1.
lesson.body:
Differentiability, as covered in the previous section, is usually discussed as a property of a function over its whole domain, but the actual test for it is always local, checked one point at a time, since the derivative at a point is itself a number tied to that specific input. A function can be differentiable at some points and not at others within the very same graph, so the precise question to ask is never simply "is f differentiable," but "is f differentiable at this particular x = a," answered by checking whether f prime of a, defined as the limit as h approaches 0 of [f(a + h) minus f(a)] divided by h, actually exists and is finite.

For piecewise functions, defined by different formulas on different intervals, this pointwise check usually comes down to comparing one sided derivatives at the seam where the formulas meet. Continuity at that seam is required first, since discontinuity alone already rules out differentiability, but continuity is not the final word; the slopes approaching from each side must also agree.

Work through f(x), defined piecewise, equal to x squared for x less than or equal to 1, and equal to 3x minus 2 for x greater than 1. First check continuity at x = 1. From the left piece, f(1) equals 1 squared, which is 1. From the right piece, the limit as x approaches 1 from above of 3x minus 2 equals 3 times 1 minus 2, which is also 1. The two sides agree and match the actual function value, so f is continuous at x = 1.

Continuity alone does not settle differentiability, so check the one sided derivatives next. On the left piece, x squared has derivative 2x, established earlier by the limit definition, so the left hand derivative at x = 1 is 2 times 1, which is 2. On the right piece, 3x minus 2 is a straight line with constant slope 3, so the right hand derivative at x = 1 is simply 3. The left hand derivative, 2, does not equal the right hand derivative, 3, so the two one sided limits in the difference quotient disagree, meaning f prime of 1 does not exist. The function is continuous at x = 1 but not differentiable there, producing a visible corner in its graph even though there is no break or jump in the curve itself.

It is worth contrasting this outcome with what would have happened if the second piece had instead been 2x minus 1. Redoing the continuity check, the right hand limit at x = 1 would be 2 times 1 minus 1, which is 1, still matching. But the right hand derivative would then be 2, the constant slope of 2x minus 1, exactly equal to the left hand derivative of 2 found above. In that version the two pieces would meet with the same value and the same slope, so f prime of 1 would exist and equal 2, no corner at all. The only difference between a smooth join and a corner is whether those two one sided derivative numbers happen to agree.

This example is the pointwise version of everything the last several sections established: differentiability at a point is decided entirely by the difference quotient limit at that single input, continuity is a necessary but not sufficient condition for it, and the moment the one sided derivatives disagree, however close the function values are, the derivative simply does not exist at that spot.
